title: मातृभाषा शिक्षणमा देखापरेका चुनौतीहरू
nepali: प्रस्तुत लेखमा नेपालको सन्दर्भमा मातृभाषा शिक्षणसँग सम्बन्धित विविध पक्षहरूको अध्ययन गरिएको छ । वि. सं. २०६८ को राष्ट्रिय जनगणनाअनुसार नेपालमा १२३ वटा भाषा अस्तित्वमा रहेका छन्, जसमध्ये माध्यम भाषाका रूपमा रहेको नेपाली भाषा ४४.६४% ले मातृभाषाका रूपमा बोल्दछन् भने ५५.३६% को मातृभाषा नेपालीबाहेक अन्य रहेको छ । नेपालको अन्तरिम संविधान (२०६३) र नेपालको संविधान २०७२ ले नेपालमा बोलिने सबै मातृभाषाहरूलाई राष्ट्रभाषाको मान्यता दिँदै नेपालमा बसोबास गर्ने प्रत्येक नेपाली समुदायलाई कानुनबमोजिम आफ्नो मातृभाषामा शिक्षा पाउने र त्यसका लागि विद्यालय तथा शैक्षिक संस्था खोल्ने र सञ्चालन गर्ने हक प्रदान गरेको छ, तर यसलाई पूर्ण रूपमा कार्यान्वयन गर्न विविध प्रकारका चुनौतीहरू रहेका छन् । यसै परिप्रेक्ष्यमा यस लेखमा नेपालमा बोलिने भाषाहरूको अवस्था, मातृभाषा शिक्षणको उद्देश्य, मातृभाषा शिक्षणमा देखापरेका समस्याहरू, मातृभाषा शिक्षणको क्षेत्रमा भएका प्रयासहरू र मातृभाषा शिक्षणमा विद्यमान समस्या निराकरण गर्न अपनाउन सकिने उपायहरू प्रस्तुत गरिएको छ । हाल नेपालमा मातृभाषा शिक्षणको क्षेत्रमा विभिन्न चुनौतीहरू देखिए तापनि लेख्यीकरणको स्तरमा आइसकेका भाषाहरूमा पाठ्यक्रम तथा पाठ्यपुस्तकहरू निर्माण गरी पठनपाठन गर्ने कार्य प्रत्येक वर्ष बढ्दै गइरहेको  छ । आफ्नो जातिको भाषा संरक्षण र सम्बद्र्धनका लागि कतिपय जातिहरू लागिपरेका छन् । प्रादेशिक स्तरमा पनि यस क्षेत्रमा महत्त्वपूर्ण कामहरू सुरु भएका छन् । नेपालमा बोलिने भाषाहरूको संरक्षण, संवद्र्धन र विकास गर्ने, मातृभाषाहरूको विकासको स्तर मापन गरी शिक्षामा प्रयोगको सम्भाव्यता अध्ययन गर्ने, भाषाहरूको अध्ययन, अनुसन्धान र अनुगमन गर्ने उद्देश्य अनुरूप वि. सं. २०७३ मा भाषा आयोग गठन भई यसले काम सुरु गरिसकेको छ । त्यसै गरी पाठ्यक्रम विकास केन्द्र, नेपाल प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठान, त्रिभुवन विश्वविद्यालय, स्थानीय निकाय लगायतका विभिन्न सरकारी तथा गैरसरकारी संस्थाहरूले नेपालमा अस्तित्वमा रहेका भाषाहरूको संरक्षण, संवद्र्धन र विकासका लागि विविध कार्यहरू गरिरहेको सन्दर्भमा यी संस्थाहरूले एकआपसमा समन्वय गरेर योजनाबद्ध रूपमा काम गर्ने हो भने मातृभाषा शिक्षणमा विद्यमान चुनौतीहरू क्रमशः कम हुँदै जाने निष्कर्ष यस लेखमा निकालिएको छ ।
american_english: In the present article, various aspects related to mother-tongue education in the context of Nepal have been studied. According to the National Population Census of 2068 B.S., 123 languages exist in Nepal, of which the Nepali language, serving as the medium of communication, is spoken as a mother tongue by 44.64%, while 55.36% have a mother tongue other than Nepali. The Interim Constitution of Nepal (2063) and the Constitution of Nepal 2072, recognizing all mother tongues spoken in Nepal as national languages, grant every Nepali community residing in Nepal the right to receive education in its mother tongue in accordance with the law and to establish and operate schools and educational institutions for that purpose, but there are various types of challenges to fully implement this. In this context, this article presents the status of languages spoken in Nepal, the objectives of mother-tongue education, the problems encountered in mother-tongue teaching, the efforts made in the field of mother-tongue education, and the measures that can be adopted to resolve the existing problems in mother-tongue teaching. Although various challenges are currently seen in the field of mother-tongue education in Nepal, the work of developing curricula and textbooks and conducting teaching and learning in languages that have reached the level of written form has been increasing every year. Several ethnic groups are actively committed to preserving and promoting their community's language. Important initiatives have also begun in this field at the provincial level. In accordance with the objectives of preserving, promoting, and developing languages spoken in Nepal, measuring the developmental level of mother tongues to study the feasibility of their use in education, and studying, researching, and monitoring languages, the Language Commission was formed in 2073 B.S. and has already started its work. Likewise, in the context where various governmental and non-governmental organizations, including the Curriculum Development Centre, Nepal Academy, Tribhuvan University, and local bodies, are carrying out various activities for the preservation, promotion, and development of languages existing in Nepal, this article concludes that if these organizations coordinate with one another and work in a planned manner, the existing challenges in mother-tongue education will gradually diminish.

informal_english: In this paper, we look at various aspects related to mother-tongue schooling across Nepal. According to the 2068 BS national census, 123 languages exist across Nepal, with 44.64% speaking Nepali—which serves as the contact language—as their mother tongue, while 55.36% have a mother tongue other than Nepali. Nepal's Interim Constitution (2063) and the 2072 Constitution recognise every mother tongue spoken in Nepal as a national language, giving every Nepali community living here the right to get educated in its mother tongue under the law and to set up and run schools and educational institutions for it, but there are all sorts of challenges to get this fully implemented. In this context, this article lays out the state of languages spoken in Nepal, the goals of mother-tongue education, the snags cropping up in mother-tongue teaching, the efforts made in the field, and the steps that can be taken to sort out the existing problems in mother-tongue teaching. Even though various challenges are currently seen in mother-tongue education in Nepal, the work of putting together curricula and textbooks and teaching in languages that have reached a written form has been increasing every year. Quite a few ethnic communities are actively keen on preserving and promoting their community's language. Important work has also kicked off in this area at the provincial level. In line with the goals of preserving, promoting, and developing languages spoken in Nepal, measuring how developed mother tongues are to see if they can be used in education, and studying, researching, and monitoring languages, the Language Commission was set up in 2073 BS and has already got to work. Along the same lines, with various government and non-government bodies like the Curriculum Development Centre, Nepal Academy, Tribhuvan University, and local councils carrying out all sorts of activities to preserve, promote, and develop languages across Nepal, this paper wraps up with the conclusion that if these groups coordinate with each other and work to a solid plan, the existing challenges in mother-tongue education will gradually ease up.
